segments.title: Why future-war comparisons need the whole task group
segments.body: Even a powerful warship can be overwhelmed when it is isolated and an opponent can mass drones and missiles for a timed attack. That vulnerability repeats an old fleet problem and does not prove that one new weapon has made large ships obsolete. Wartime navies form task groups so ships can share sensors, weapons, logistics, and defensive coverage. The whole formation is the useful unit for judging whether an attack can succeed.

evidence.note: An isolated ship facing a coordinated mass attack and the mutual support and sustainment available within a wartime task group.

segments.summary: A drone or missile salvo against an isolated warship tests a different problem from attacking a mutually supporting task group.

segments.title: Undersea drone concepts meet communications and terrain
segments.body: Reliable communication with submerged submarines remains difficult even for advanced navies, and richer coordination among submarines and underwater vehicles raises still harder engineering problems. Hardwired links introduce their own risks because cables can tangle as currents move vehicles around real seabed terrain. Autonomous underwater systems already have useful mine-countermeasure roles, although that experience does not make a networked submarine wolfpack mature. Its deployment timetable depends on solving those engineering problems.

evidence.note: Limited reliable submerged communications, cable entanglement, currents and seabed terrain, and existing mine-countermeasure work with autonomous underwater vehicles.

segments.summary: A proposed drone-carrier submarine wolfpack becomes a case study in underwater communications, coordination, cables, currents, and seabed terrain.

segments.title: Queen Bee and HMS Argus place naval drones in an interwar lineage
segments.body: Modern naval drones have roots in interwar British experiments with the Queen Bee target system. The target aircraft flew from converted HMS Argus, identified as the world's first drone carrier, with that role dated to 1939, possibly 1938. Remotely controlled aircraft existed even earlier. The long development of aerial drones supports caution about how quickly more ambitious submarine-drone wolfpacks will become operational.

evidence.note: Queen Bee target aircraft aboard HMS Argus, uncertain 1938 or 1939 dating, earlier remote-control aviation, and caution about development times.

segments.summary: British target-drone experiments aboard HMS Argus show that remote-control aviation has a much longer history than today's fleet-autonomy debate suggests.

segments.title: Hypersonic labels can obscure the real threat
segments.body: An isolated air-defence ship facing a mass raid may depend on electronic warfare spoofing enough threats to leave missiles available for the remaining attackers. Calling a weapon hypersonic does not explain whether it reaches that speed throughout its flight or only during one part. The comparison here places the lower threshold around Mach 5 or Mach 7 and treats Mach 20 as a much more extreme proposition than a ballistic arrival around Mach 7. The forecast discounts Mach 20 attacks within the next ten years apart from hypothetical space-based kinetic weapons. These speed estimates underpin a criticism of inflated performance claims that prevent a useful assessment of fleet defence.

evidence.note: Electronic warfare preserving interceptor stocks, variable use of hypersonic thresholds, partial-flight speeds, and scepticism about near-term Mach 20 attacks.

segments.summary: Electronic warfare and missile stocks matter in a mass raid, while a hypersonic label alone says too little about a weapon's flight profile.

segments.title: A Queen Elizabeth group shows post-Cold War fleet assumptions
segments.body: The group around HMS Queen Elizabeth combined British and American F-35Bs with frigates, Type 45 destroyers, an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, allied escorts, and supply ships. The British aircraft purchase had not kept pace with the carrier program, so American aircraft helped fill the deck. A future balance of 18 to 24 British F-35Bs for air defence, with drones taking much of the strike role, is offered as a workable minimum for one carrier group. Every major capability was represented, although the formation remained thin after decades of planning for technological superiority and discretionary wars.

evidence.note: Queen Elizabeth's mixed British and American F-35B group, escorts and supply ships, a proposed 18 to 24 F-35 air-defence complement, and post-Cold War assumptions.

segments.summary: A British carrier deployment illustrates how a post-Cold War task group could contain every major capability while remaining thin in ship and aircraft numbers.

segments.title: Modern frigates and destroyers still perform the cruising role
segments.body: Distant patrols, diplomatic events, and showing the flag are traditional cruising tasks performed by modern frigates and destroyers. In that peacetime sense, both types function as cruisers. Their frigate or destroyer labels chiefly describe what they are expected to do in war. Frigates usually concentrate on anti-submarine warfare, while destroyers usually specialize in air defence and may carry another capability such as land attack.

evidence.note: Peacetime cruising duties and the usual wartime ASW or air-defence specialization behind modern escort labels.

segments.summary: Peacetime presence missions make modern escorts cruisers in function, while their frigate or destroyer labels describe wartime specialization.

segments.title: Sea Ceptor changes the Type 45 missile mix
segments.body: The Type 45's intended secondary land-attack role included Mark 41 vertical-launch cells for weapons such as Tomahawk. The upgrade described here instead adds CAMM, or Sea Ceptor, for short-range air defence. Taking that role away from Aster 15 allows more Aster 30 missiles in the existing Sea Viper load. The expected total rises to 72 missiles, a useful increase that is still judged short of the magazine depth needed.

evidence.note: Proposed Mark 41 and Tomahawk role, Sea Ceptor replacing Aster 15's short-range function, more Aster 30, and an expected 72-missile total.

segments.summary: Adding Sea Ceptor would free more of the Type 45's existing missile load for Aster 30, while its earlier land-attack ambition remains unfulfilled.

segments.title: Type 23 cuts and the size of a light frigate
segments.body: The Type 23 was intended to provide numbers at the end of the Cold War and replace Leander-class frigates. The procurement account gives 24 planned ships, 18 ordered, and 16 built after post-Cold War cuts. Its description as a light frigate also needs a sense of scale. At just under 5,000 tons, it was close in size to the Second World War Arethusa-class light cruisers, estimated here to differ by only about 400 tons.

evidence.note: Type 23 replacement role, corrected 24 planned / 18 ordered / 16 built figures, and approximate Arethusa-class displacement comparison.

segments.summary: The Type 23 example combines shrinking procurement numbers with a light-frigate hull approaching the size of a wartime light cruiser.

segments.title: Modern warships are power plants and data centres at sea
segments.body: Sensitive sensors collect faint returns amid large amounts of clutter. Computing power separates those returns from background signals and turns them into useful tracks and firing solutions. Larger warships can carry more sensors, processing equipment, and electrical generation, which helps them detect threats farther away. A modern warship is therefore much like a power plant and data centre inside a seagoing hull, with its visible weapons dependent on that infrastructure. Earlier detection and mutual support are treated as continuing lessons from the Second World War.

evidence.note: Computing to distinguish faint returns from clutter, electrical generation, and the benefits of earlier threat detection and shared fleet capabilities.

segments.summary: Growing sensors and engagement ranges make electrical power and signal processing as important to a warship's capability as its visible weapons.

segments.title: A task group distributes capabilities across large and small ships
segments.body: Samantha Carter in Stargate SG-1 illustrates the fictional habit of giving one person almost unlimited scientific and engineering abilities. Naval stories similarly tend to place command and every technical solution aboard one ship. Since the Second World War, task groups have distributed capabilities across several vessels. That requires a mixture of ship sizes because powerful radars and computers still need substantial space. Adding small ships alone cannot replace every function of a larger hull.

evidence.note: Samantha Carter's fictional versatility, single-ship storytelling, and the real requirement for mixed task groups with space for major radars and computers.

segments.summary: A mixed task group distributes sensors, weapons, and specialist expertise across ships of different sizes.

segments.title: Local radar processing reduces a task group's emissions
segments.body: A task group may have good reasons to use a surface ship's radar as well as airborne early warning. The ship operating that radar needs enough computing power to process what it receives. Sending all the data elsewhere would require ships to communicate continuously across the formation's operational spacing. That traffic creates detectable emissions and can reveal the group's position. Laser links also have to work across the real distances between ships at sea.

evidence.note: Emission security and the difficulty of continuous data exchange across operational distances, including laser links.
Local radar processing reduces the need to distribute raw data through detectable communications.

segments.summary: Processing radar data aboard the transmitting ship limits the continuous communications that could reveal a task group's location.

segments.title: Task-group spacing keeps weapons clear to engage
segments.body: Ships close together in a publicity photograph are following a special formation order. Operational spacing is measured in miles and reflects the weapons the ships must use. Placing an allied ship too close can block a gun's line of fire or prevent another engagement. Wider separation lets several ships attack a threat without masking one another. A photograph at that spacing would reduce most of the ships to distant dots.

evidence.note: Photographic formations, separation in miles, and examples of nearby friendly ships obstructing weapons fire.

segments.summary: The gaps between ships allow their weapons to support one another, even though publicity photographs show a much tighter formation.

segments.title: Satellite reconnaissance still has gaps in wartime
segments.body: Even the United States' extensive satellite network has gaps in peacetime coverage. War adds deliberate attempts to disable or destroy satellites. Possible methods include missiles fired from the ground, blinding with directed radiation, or a collision presented as an accident during a disposal manoeuvre. A fleet's position therefore cannot simply be assumed to remain visible through a continuous, secure satellite picture.

evidence.note: Peacetime gaps and possible wartime satellite loss through missiles, blinding, or a collision disguised as a failed disposal manoeuvre.

segments.summary: Peacetime coverage gaps and wartime attacks on satellites limit the assumption that an enemy always knows where a fleet is.

segments.title: Red Sea and Black Sea lessons depend on confined geography
segments.body: A force operating 200 to 250 nautical miles offshore has an enormous search area available in the Atlantic, Pacific, or Indian Ocean. The same distance leaves few possible positions in the Black Sea and may be impossible across parts of the Red Sea. Map scale therefore changes how easily a ship can hide, manoeuvre, and stay outside coastal weapon range. Combat reports from confined seas need that geographic context before they are applied to ocean warfare.

evidence.note: The restricted space available 200 to 250 nautical miles offshore in confined seas, compared with the much larger search areas of the major oceans.

segments.summary: Confined seas sharply reduce the offshore space in which ships can hide, so their combat lessons do not transfer unchanged to the Atlantic, Pacific, or Indian oceans.

segments.title: Red Sea attacks exposed a crossing-target problem
segments.body: Task-group air defences had concentrated on attacks coming into the defended formation. Red Sea operations exposed a different geometry, with missiles travelling across a ship's engagement area. A weapon crossing the area presents a different interception problem from one approaching the task group itself. This is a specific lesson from those engagements that remains useful even though the surrounding waters differ from an open ocean.

evidence.note: Red Sea difficulty engaging missiles crossing the engagement area after a long focus on attacks directed into a task group.

segments.summary: A missile travelling across a ship's engagement area can test defences differently from an attack aimed into its task group.

segments.title: Black Sea Fleet losses and unequal institutional priority
segments.body: The Black Sea Fleet's condition is questioned alongside the geographic constraints on its operations. One proposed explanation is that post-Cold War leadership failures and corruption damaged it more than the Northern and Pacific fleets. Those other fleets may have received some protection from their nuclear-submarine responsibilities, since nuclear weapons and submarines retained comparatively greater funding and oversight. That oversight is explicitly judged imperfect, and the other fleets had problems of their own. Assuming all Russian fleets were in the same condition could therefore distort the lessons drawn from Black Sea losses.

evidence.note: Interpretation of Black Sea neglect and corruption, with qualified comparisons to Northern and Pacific nuclear-fleet funding and oversight.

segments.summary: Differences in funding, oversight, and nuclear-submarine responsibilities offer a qualified explanation for the Black Sea Fleet's condition.

segments.title: Why a convoy can be harder to find in an ocean
segments.body: A convoy places many ships at one point in a large ocean, while dispersed merchant ships create many separate points an enemy can encounter. In the Atlantic or Pacific, the convoy can disappear within the available search area. Enclosed or nearly enclosed waters offer much less room to manoeuvre and make routes easier to observe. The contrast helps explain why protecting trade in the Red Sea presents a different problem. Distance also affects which sensors and weapons can find and engage the ships.

evidence.note: First and Second World War convoy concentration, ocean concealment, constrained trade routes, and the effect of distance on sensors and weapons.

segments.summary: Convoy concentration can help ships avoid discovery in a wide ocean, while enclosed seas make movement easier to track.

segments.title: Future warfare will fuse current technology with older lessons
segments.body: Current drone and missile experience belongs in any forecast of naval warfare. Older wars still matter because they expose recurring problems in detection, range, coordination, and force concentration. Cheap drones can become an acute threat during amphibious operations or in short-range waters. Ocean operations impose different demands on endurance and targeting, so future fleets must account for both environments.

evidence.note: Combining historical lessons with current weapons experience, with cheap drone swarms especially relevant to amphibious operations and short-range waters.

segments.summary: Current drone and missile experience matters, but distance and mission determine whether a weapon that dominates a confined littoral remains decisive at ocean scale.

segments.title: Anti-ship ballistic missiles carry targeting and escalation risks
segments.body: Hypersonic weapons are judged expensive and scarce, although newer designs are becoming more viable. The DF-21 example raises a separate concern: a large salvo still looks like a ballistic-missile launch, creating a risk of nuclear escalation during an existing war. Positive identification does not remove every fear about the launch's target or purpose. Finding and tracking the carrier group is also essential because the ships keep moving. The targeting example uses an estimated flight time of 45 minutes to an hour to illustrate how far ahead the attacker must predict the target's position.

evidence.note: Expensive hypersonic weapons, improving newer designs, the DF-21 escalation example, and an estimated 45-minute to one-hour flight used to illustrate moving-target prediction.

segments.summary: The DF-21 example combines the risk of misreading a mass ballistic launch with the need to keep tracking a moving carrier group.

segments.title: Ocean distance changes the loitering-munition problem
segments.body: Small loitering munitions with about 150 miles of range and a few hours of endurance have useful opportunities where a ship's route and timing are known. Finding a fleet hundreds of nautical miles offshore is a different demand. In a hypothetical Taiwan operation, a force offshore from Taiwan would be farther still from a mainland Chinese launcher. For a reusable aircraft, the range example budgets roughly 500 nautical miles for the outward and return legs before any loitering. Indirect routing also costs range but helps conceal the launch ship's position. These demands help explain the difficult long-range requirements placed on American carrier-drone development.

evidence.note: Illustrative drone ranges and endurance, a hypothetical Taiwan scenario, return-flight and loiter requirements, and launch-position concealment. Distance figures are approximate and use both miles and nautical miles.

segments.summary: A weapon with impressive littoral range may still lack the endurance to search for a moving fleet hundreds of nautical miles offshore and return without revealing its launcher.

segments.title: Layered attacks must defeat layered fleet defences
segments.body: Drones and fast missiles are expected to form part of future naval warfare. Comparing one weapon with one ship leaves out how an actual attack combines systems to penetrate a battle group's defences. The defenders must assess that combination and arrange their own layers to meet it. Guns, missiles, and lasers belong in that assessment because the defence has to deal with several kinds of threat.

evidence.note: Combined attack systems against a battle group's defensive layers, including the continued place of guns alongside missiles and lasers.

segments.summary: Drones, missiles, guns, sensors, and electronic warfare interact as combinations, so simple weapon-beats-ship comparisons miss the structure of an actual engagement.

segments.title: Counter-drone guns and jammers in the Strait of Hormuz
segments.body: The Strait of Hormuz provides a confined-water example where cheap drones could swarm a ship. Rapid-fire 57 mm or 76 mm guns are proposed as a way to engage small drones at a reasonable cost before they reach the hull. The recommendation is for at least four such mounts, supported by radar, electronic warfare, and countermeasures. Putting enough shells into the approach path applies a familiar Second World War principle. Jammers and guns are expected to handle many small-drone attacks, with point-defence or larger missiles available when needed.

evidence.note: A Strait of Hormuz example, 57 mm and 76 mm guns, a recommendation for at least four mounts, electronic warfare, and missile backup.

segments.summary: A proposed defence against cheap drones combines several rapid-fire guns with electronic warfare and missiles, keeping cost per engagement in view.

segments.title: Smarter drones create larger systems or fragile kill chains
segments.body: A drone able to evade layered defences needs speed, sensors, processing power, and the energy to support them. Adding those capabilities increases both size and cost. Remote control can move the computation to a satellite-linked data centre, although this creates dependence on communications and ground infrastructure. Burying a command centre does not remove the vulnerability of satellite links and ground stations. Every added connection gives an opponent another place to interrupt the kill chain.

evidence.note: Size and cost of onboard sensors and computation, offboard satellite links and data centres, and vulnerabilities in ground stations and command links.

segments.summary: Adding speed, autonomy, sensors, and evasive behaviour makes a drone larger and costlier, while moving those functions ashore creates vulnerable communications links.

segments.title: Future uncrewed sloops may grow to destroyer-escort size
segments.body: 'Sloop' is the preferred name here for a future uncrewed partner, with 'loyal kayak' another term used in the debate. Range, seakeeping, and enough weapons to justify those capabilities are expected to push independent vessels toward 2,000 to 3,000 tons. First-generation designs may be closer to a few hundred or 1,000 tons, but growth toward Second World War destroyer or escort size is predicted to follow quickly. Smaller uncrewed craft would still be carried and recovered by parent ships. The forecast therefore leaves roles for both large partners and small deployable boats.

evidence.note: A preference for the name sloop, the forecast of 2,000- to 3,000-ton independent escorts, initially smaller designs, and separate small recoverable craft.

segments.summary: Range, seakeeping, speed, and useful weapon capacity push independent uncrewed escorts toward roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tons.

segments.title: Uncrewed sloops multiply anti-submarine coverage
segments.body: A frigate accompanied by two uncrewed sloops could coordinate three towed sonar arrays. The proposed partners would normally operate with a crewed ship rather than patrol alone. A crewed helicopter could similarly hunt with three or four uncrewed aircraft supporting it. These combinations would restore numbers and increase coverage across the large areas involved in anti-submarine warfare.

evidence.note: A frigate and two partners with three towed arrays, plus a helicopter supported by three or four uncrewed aircraft.

segments.summary: Pairing a frigate with uncrewed surface and air vehicles can put more sonar arrays and aircraft into the search area without duplicating full crews.

segments.title: An uncrewed sloop could draw missiles away from crewed ships
segments.body: A commander facing incoming hypersonic missiles could send an uncrewed vessel at an angle toward the threat. The proposed decoy would enlarge its radar return while the crewed ships reduced theirs. Accepting the possible loss of the uncrewed partner would protect people and the ships carrying them. Larger uncrewed vessels could carry more supporting equipment, while dedicated support ships could deploy and recover smaller assets. This partnership resembles the loyal-wingman concept in aviation, scaled up for warships.

evidence.note: Conditional sacrifice of an uncrewed asset, enlarged radar return, reduced crewed-ship returns, and larger vessels supporting uncrewed systems.

segments.summary: A proposed radar-decoy role uses an uncrewed partner's expendability to complicate attacks on the crewed ships.

segments.title: A carrier group gains depth from an uncrewed escort screen
segments.body: One proposed carrier group gives four uncrewed partners to a large cruiser-like combatant and two to each of four Arleigh Burke-class destroyers. Those twelve sloops join five crewed escorts, producing seventeen ships around the carrier. The carrier can concentrate on aviation while the escorts support the additional surface vessels. A submarine seeking to reach the central ships would have to pass more towed arrays, helicopters, and other systems. The example treats uncrewed technology as a source of defensive capability that also complicates the attacker's task.

evidence.note: A hypothetical large surface combatant with four partners and four Burkes with two each, giving seventeen escorts and more ASW obstacles around a carrier.

segments.summary: A force-design sketch pairs each large surface combatant with several uncrewed sloops to create a much wider defensive screen around a carrier.

segments.title: Uncrewed convoy escorts must keep pace with the fleet
segments.body: A future merchant convoy might have one or two crewed warships, such as an air-defence escort and an anti-submarine escort, supported by four or five uncrewed vessels. That balance recalls the numbers used in Second World War convoy protection. A stripped-down vessel around 1,000 tons, compared here with a Flower-class corvette, remains a possibility. The objection is speed: an uncrewed partner limited to about 18 knots would constrain a formation whose crewed ships can manoeuvre at more than 30 knots.

evidence.note: One or two crewed convoy escorts with four or five uncrewed partners, a possible Flower-like 1,000-ton design, and the 18-knot versus 30-plus-knot comparison.

segments.summary: A convoy could combine a few crewed specialists with several uncrewed escorts, but the proposed partners still need enough speed to manoeuvre with the fleet.

segments.title: Missile-carrying uncrewed ships need room for repair crews
segments.body: Future uncrewed partners are expected to carry missiles and may offer landing or refuelling points for uncrewed aircraft if sufficient automation becomes possible. They are likely to need basic accommodation, including toilets, for maintainers sent aboard. Wartime reliability must allow for enemies actively trying to break the equipment as well as ordinary failures. A vessel forced to return home for repairs can be as unavailable to the operation as one that has been destroyed. Keeping engineering teams aboard the crewed ships and providing access to their partners would permit some repairs at sea.

evidence.note: Possible missile trucks and automated aviation facilities, accommodation for maintainers, hostile damage, and the operational loss caused by returning home for repair.

segments.summary: Missile and aviation-support roles bring maintenance demands that favour access and basic facilities for temporary human crews.

segments.title: Recoverable boats and independent ships need different repair access
segments.body: Small uncrewed boats can be lifted aboard a parent ship or recovered through a ramp. Its engineering team can then take the equipment apart and repair it. Larger independent vessels are designed to go to sea without being carried in this way. Their maintenance access instead needs to allow a team to transfer by helicopter or boat and work aboard. That difference separates recoverable equipment from an uncrewed ship that must remain serviceable at sea.

evidence.note: Hoisting or ramp recovery for small boats, contrasted with helicopter or boat transfer of maintainers to larger independent ships.

segments.summary: A parent ship can recover and dismantle a small uncrewed boat, while an independent vessel needs access for an engineering team to come aboard.

segments.title: Canal transits could require crews aboard uncrewed ships
segments.body: Access for maintenance also creates a security problem if unauthorized people can board an uncrewed vessel. Constrained passages such as the Suez Canal could encourage daylight transits and close protection by crewed escorts. In that setting, the crewed ships would protect the uncrewed partners from boarding. Another option is to place a temporary transit crew aboard, with Royal Marines and sailors suggested for a British vessel. These are possible arrangements whose details would depend on how the ships develop.

evidence.note: Possible daylight Suez transits, protection against hostile boarding, and Royal Marines with sailors as a temporary transit crew.

segments.summary: A vessel that sails without a permanent crew may still need human guards or a temporary crew during a vulnerable canal passage.

segments.title: Force Z shows how mistakes shape weapon effectiveness
segments.body: The sinking of Prince of Wales and Repulse illustrates an argument that success in war depends heavily on making fewer mistakes than the enemy. In this account, Japanese aircraft found the ships on their return leg while low on fuel and without self-defence weapons. An RAF message saying that no aircraft were available meant strike or combat-support aircraft, while a squadron of fighters remained ready in Singapore. The Royal Navy understood the message to exclude fighters as well, giving it a reason to maintain emission silence instead of requesting cover. The counterfactual judgment is that Repulse's evasive manoeuvring, combined with fighter intervention, would probably have allowed her to survive.

evidence.note: Force Z aircraft search, the claimed RAF-message misunderstanding and unrequested fighter support, followed by a qualified Repulse-survival counterfactual.

segments.summary: The Force Z example connects Japanese reconnaissance luck and an ambiguous air-support message to a qualified argument about Repulse's chances with fighter cover.

segments.title: Eighteen bombers versus a battleship of the same vintage
segments.body: An interwar cost comparison put a battleship against roughly eighteen medium bombers. The test was whether those aircraft could be guaranteed to sink a battleship of similar vintage. Using a much older First World War ship would change the comparison. The answer remained uncertain, which limits how much the price ratio alone could establish. The example supports caution about wonder-weapon claims, since defensive sensors and other systems improve alongside faster attacking weapons.

evidence.note: Approximate eighteen-bomber cost comparison, the requirement for similar-vintage ships and aircraft, and improving defences alongside faster weapons.

segments.summary: The interwar bomber comparison depended on matching contemporary aircraft against a contemporary battleship, and still produced an uncertain answer.

segments.title: Defence marketing rewards new wonder-weapon narratives
segments.body: Defence manufacturers have incentives to promote new equipment and build a public case for buying it. The criticism here is that paid promotion and company publications can steer coverage toward new systems while mature countermeasures receive less attention. Lasers attract interest as a future answer to drones, even though light rapid-fire artillery is also considered a possible defence. The argument supports laser development while questioning reliance on systems before they work. Sponsorship can make economic sense for creators and media companies, and rewriting a press release costs less than original research. Those incentives still need to be considered when assessing a claim about a weapon's value.

evidence.note: Criticism of paid defence promotion, the contrast between gun countermeasures and future lasers, and the cost incentives behind sponsorship and press-release coverage.

segments.summary: Claims about new weapons need to be tested against who benefits from the story and whether cheaper existing systems already address part of the threat.

segments.title: A large surface combatant can add task-group magazine depth
segments.body: The proposed large surface combatant discussed in this video could contribute to a carrier group through its missile capacity. A hull of that size would be particularly useful in this argument if it carried more vertical-launch cells. Those additional missiles would deepen the formation's magazine for sustained fighting. That advantage matters especially while reloading VLS cells at sea remains an unresolved problem in the assessment presented here.

evidence.note: Conditional value of a large carrier-group escort with additional VLS cells, greater magazine depth, and unresolved reloading at sea.

segments.summary: The naval value of the proposed large surface combatant depends on how many additional missiles it could contribute to a carrier task group.

segments.title: Ocean seakeeping puts a floor under uncrewed ship size
segments.body: The strongest forecast concerns growth in the size of independent uncrewed escorts. Requirements for range, speed, and seakeeping are expected to push them beyond early thousand-ton designs, toward roughly 2,000 and eventually 2,700 tons. Advanced stabilization does not remove the need to cope with the sea itself. Other aspects of future fleet design remain open to debate. Ocean operations extend beyond individual regions and require enough hull volume to carry the fuel for those distances.

evidence.note: A comparatively firm forecast of escort growth from seakeeping and range requirements, with other design choices left open and ocean distance increasing fuel demand.

segments.summary: The final forecast rests on a physical constraint: ocean-going vessels need enough size for fuel, range, speed, payload, and survival in real seas.

segments.title: Small solar-powered craft have useful but limited sensor roles
segments.body: Small solar-powered craft can travel around the world while performing limited sensor tasks. Their endurance is useful within that narrow role. They remain exposed to accidental collection in fishing nets and other damage at sea. The example qualifies size-based fleet forecasts by preserving a place for small specialist craft alongside larger fighting vessels.

evidence.note: Solar-powered craft on limited sensor missions, including the risk of collection in fishing nets, disappearance, and damage.

segments.summary: Long-range solar-powered sensor craft retain a useful niche, with exposure to fishing gear and other damage limiting what can be assumed of them.
